chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from al-Husayn ibn Muhammad from Mu'alla ibn Muhammad from al-Washsha' from Aban from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Abdillah from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

Imam Ali (peace be upon him), when two men came to him with evidence and their witnesses were equal in justice and equal in number, would cast lots between them to determine whose oath would be taken.
He (the Imam) would say, 'O God, Lord of the seven heavens, whichever of them is entitled to the right, grant it to him.'
Then he would assign the right to the one whose oath was taken, once he had sworn.
ai.seo_question: How did Imam Ali rule when two parties had equal evidence in court?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* details the specific judicial mechanism of *al-qur'a* (casting lots) employed by Imam Ali (peace be upon him) to resolve disputes where the evidence of two parties was in perfect equilibrium. By invoking divine will through an oath, this practice highlights the Shia scholarly understanding of using tangible means to ascertain truth when rational deduction yields parity, reflecting the practical application of justice in early Islamic jurisprudence.
